Possible workarounds that have come to mind:

1. Automate the manual work you spend on corrections (add default region and business line, create specific reports for copy-paste into the manual EIB journal, fix validation...)
2. Don't post paid VAT to 6715, but allocate it to the invoice spend account along with the net amount (as we do for non-IC invoices). Then automate corrections if 6715 is highly needed (specific reports correlated with EIB).
3. Each time create a separate supplier invoice for paid VAT amount to treat it as paid VAT for non-IC invoices (but in this case we need to test the settlement carefully).

We could arrange the meeting to think over together.

Hi all - from a DAC7 perspective, there is no obligation to collect, verify, or report the seller’s email address. Strictly speaking, we are not mandated to collect it or provide it to the tax authorities as any handling of email addresses falls outside the scope of DAC7. This is a general privacy question, and not DAC7 driven. Thus, from a DAC7 perspective, there is no issue for drivers and couriers to have a separate email address, or the access to change it as needed. 

I see the email address being relevant for us in the following situation in the context of the DAC7: 

(1) informing sellers about the applicability of DAC7 and what it means for them (e.g. upon onboarding), and

(2) providing them with their annual individual report prior to submitting the consolidated DAC7 report to the tax authorities.

(3) General communication e.g. request of further documents and details, etc.

The problem occurs when an initial interaction is replied to - we submit a {{draft}} case and store the interaction reply. Once the case is submitted (state changes to {{open}}), the initial interaction is no longer valid due to a changed state, and the event state change [handler|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/a5c0cf47e890446d66b56ada6a60eedfa5ff82ce/src/platform/cs/customer_support/main/listeners/SupportCaseEventStateChangeListener.ts#L120] tries to invalidate it. However, the interaction is already replied (means not pending anymore), in the event that follows issue submitting and cannot be invalidated anymore (*this is what was causing alerting and extra logging due to false attempts to invalidate it*). To improve this, we need to either review the order in which we store events (store the interaction reply first) or keep the submitted case in its current state (e.g., draft, so interaction could remain valid) and only allow the case state to change in the interaction replied event.

Summary of notes from meeting with Merve, Kristjan and also after brainstorming with Lachlan:

* Heavy on Privacy - DPIA required, automated decision-making is always tricky, human review (after suspension seems fine), transparency of the logic and consequences (simplified in the App but ready to disclose more details upon request), right to object, right to erase, straightforward dispute mechanism, (longer?) storage of IoT data in case of disputes.
* Notification (in-App and email) before score is live.
* Can we ensure Bolt obtains the data from Lematics or other provider quickly enough in case of disputes or scrutiny from authorities?
* Suspension/banning remains independent from score, but will there be an exclusively score-based suspension/ban in addition to it?
* Negative consequences/punishments attract scrutiny from users and authorities. Positive consequences/incentives are as a rule harmless.
* Education campaigns? Tips to improve score? How/when is the score improved again? Staying with a low score for long without a way out except renting more Bolt Drive cars may negatively affect user experience and PR. Time for score to reset is also relevant.
* Confirm score is fully controlled by Bolt - e.g., no score by next user or 3P.
* Are thresholds for speeding and harsh driving affecting the score flexible enough? How do we decide harsh acceleration, braking, cornering is harsh? Are there any references from rules, car manufacturers or industry standards?
* Low score even without negative consequences affect the user experience and may create friction.
* Presumption of innocence should be even greater. E.g., if a user complaints and there’s doubt about whether the blocking was fair, Bolt should refrain from blocking. The goal should be to avoid customers who could threat Bolt’s business or the safety of others.

SQL



{noformat}with cte as
    (select fsc.support_case_id,
                    fsc.support_case_isasue_submitted_ts_utc,
                    fsc.support_case_created_date_utc,
                    fsc.support_case_order_id,
                    fsc.support_case_city_id,
                    fsc.support_case_user_id,
                    fro.order_state,
                    COALESCE(frot.client_rating_created_ts, fro.try_to_retry_until_ts) as finished_or_cancelled_ts,
                    case
                        when support_case_isasue_submitted_ts_utc <
                             COALESCE(frot.client_rating_created_ts, fro.try_to_retry_until_ts) then 'live'
                        else 'non-live' end                                            as is_live_order


    from core_models.fact_support_case fsc

        INNER JOIN core_models.fact_rides_order as fro
                                 ON fro.order_id = fsc.support_case_order_id
                                     AND fro.order_city_id = fsc.support_case_city_id
                                     AND fro.user_id = fsc.support_case_user_id
                                     AND fro.order_state IN ('finished', 'cancelled')
                                     AND fro.created_date_local >= DATE ('2025-01-01')
    INNER JOIN core_models.fact_rides_order_try as frot
ON frot.order_id = fro.order_id
    AND frot.order_city_id = fro.order_city_id
    AND frot.order_try_state IN ('client_cancelled','finished')
    AND frot.created_date_local >= DATE ('2025-01-01')

where fsc.support_case_created_date_utc >= DATE ('2025-01-01')

  AND fsc.support_case_state NOT IN ('draft'
    , 'duplicate')
  AND fsc.support_case_order_id is NOT NULL
  AND fsc.support_case_user_type = 'rider'
  AND fsc.support_case_user_persona = 'rider'
  AND fsc.support_case_communication_channel = 'inapp_chat'
  AND fsc.is_incoming_support_case = true

    )

select
    COALESCE(i.issue_key,'no_issue_key_detected'),
    count(distinct cte.support_case_id) as nr_cases,
    SUM(COUNT(DISTINCT cte.support_case_id)) OVER () AS total_cases_count,
    round(count(distinct cte.support_case_id)*1.00 /  SUM(COUNT(DISTINCT cte.support_case_id)) OVER (),2)  as proportion


from cte

LEFT JOIN core_models.dim_support_case_issue_key as i
    ON i.support_case_id = cte.support_case_id
        AND i.is_issue_key_active = true
            AND i.support_case_created_date_utc >= DATE('2025-01-01')


where cte.is_live_order = 'live'

group by 1
order by 2 DESC

LIMIT 100
{noformat}

Hi [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] ,

Thanks for the questions. Adding comments below:

>this solution will be integrated into *the Bolt Food app,* which means registered Bolt users may explore the Dine-in restaurants and options via existing tooling, see the menus.

Correct. The product is meant to be used by registered users inside Bolt Food app. We will have a separate tab next to Home, Stores, Search etc. When clicking this tab, users will be able to discover various categories and lists of restaurants, see advertised offers. Eventually, they end up on specific restaurant’s profile page to discover the details of the offers (discounts, lunch offers, set menu offers, event offers), see menu, explore images and other content. Our app will also offer Bolt Food users to pay using Bolt Food app that will enable users access the discount offers and cashback rewards.

>However, will there be an option to be a Guest user, i.e., if the user does not want to register with Bolt, but wants to explore options, book the reservation and enjoy dine-in experience?

Not in the app, no. Eventually, we will add a web flow that will allow users to discover DineOut restaurants over the web; however, features like booking a table or paying will require authentication.

>Am I correct that in case of Bolt users making a reservation via the Bolt Food app, Bolt will collect user’s details about time of the reservation, restaurant and its address, notes and number of people in Admin and also store/show this info into the Bolt Food app? Would it work this way or would it be just an integration where Bolt does not show/store these details?

Here we need to split between MVP/early stage scope and long-term scope.

# For MVP, we don’t plan to build any table and reservation management tooling ourselves, nor do we plan to integrate with any existing table and reservation management tool. Instead, we will just forward users to relevant parts of restaurants' websites where our users can continue with table booking flow. 
# In future, we can consider either building our own tooling or acquire an existing operator. This will results in us to collecting table booking related data and also show it to the user in the app as a confirmation. 

>Am I correct that we will share these ratings and feedbacks with these restaurants as we currently do?

Not exactly in the way we do it now. The plan for MVP is that we show more detailed ratings - Bolt rating (customer will it after every DineOut payment), Google and TripAdvisor ratings.

>Am I correct that the tips will be facilitated via Bolt Food app payment solutions or will there be an integration with external providers where users may leave a tip without Bolt’s facilitation?

Correct, tips payment will be facilitated via Bolt Food app payment solution. However, we assume that most of restaurants will ask us to remove tips from the checkout, because they wouldn’t want to have tips transferred to their bank account and hit with different taxes (VAT, income and social taxes) if they had to pay it out to waiters.

>Once you start working on this marketing initiative, our team needs to be involved to ensure we have an option to send these comms to all users across all platforms. There should not be an issue, but we need to make sure it’s done correctly.

 Sure, please consider the plan to go live around September 2025.

>Am I correct that these ads would *not be targeted* to specific users on social media rather than to untargeted audience?
We can discuss details in few months when we will be closer to the launch. Generally, we don’t want to spend on customer acquisition and instead rely on reusing our current customer base. So the question is which are the best channels to achieve this goal (e.g. PR, newsletters, in-app notifications, in-app design/UI, social media posts, influencer posts, ads)?

Hi [~accountid:6352bddb13f37118d7258a9a] - I have reviewed your responses and my high-level thoughts are below.

* A GFT contact would be [~accountid:712020:338dfd87-ef5d-40bb-b10d-871b880aa66d] - looping them in for visibility.
* Subject to additional context, I would generally advise against this from a Privacy POV because:
** Selfie checks are a sensitive area in the EU as they impact whether drivers are able to access the platform (i.e., if a driver fails the check, they are potentially prevented from using their account). Even though they are a sensible initiative overall, increasing the frequency of these checks can increase the risk profile in this context.
** We need to consider data minimisation here (i.e., processing no more data about users than is strictly necessary). In this case, asking drivers to verify too frequently could be seen as disproportionate. 
** We also need to keep in mind the accountability principle under privacy law. If we introduce too many ‘random’ searches, there is a risk that we would not be able to accurately explain their frequency to a regulator if the regulator had questions about selfie checks.
** I assume every 7 days or/and every 50 trips is the frequency adopted in other EU countries? If so, please note that for operational reasons, we generally advise against adopting country-specific / localised approaches (i.e., we prefer consistent positions across countries) unless we have a strong reason to do so.
* +*However*+, we could potentially go ahead with this if there is a *_strong_* reason to do so. As such:
** I would need to see the proposed frequency of the selfie trips / more information of the proposed ‘randomness’.
** I would also need to see the letters from the ITD / understand the context a bit more, as currently I still do not have visibility on why this is urgent.

*Option 1: Direct Mobile App Control*

* *Architecture:*
** The Bolt Driver app directly integrates the Digitax Android SDK.
** All logic for controlling the taximeter (start trip, end trip, fare updates) resides within the Bolt Driver App.
** The app communicates locally (Bluetooth/wired) with the Taximeter using the SDK, which handles the COMMTAX2 protocol.
** After communication with Taximeter, Bolt Driver app should store results of communication on Bolt backend side.
* *Pros:*
** Follows the likely intended integration pattern using the Digitax SDK ({{X-One_Android_System_Features_R1.4.pdf}} mentions SDK use for user apps).
** Keeps taximeter interaction self-contained within the device environment.
** No need for real-time command communication between backend and app for taximeter functions.
* *Cons:*
** Places all taximeter control logic within the mobile app, which might be contrary to the goal of centralizing logic on the backend.
** Requires significant development effort within the Bolt Driver App to integrate and use the Digitax SDK correctly.
** Doesn't allow for direct backend initiation or control of trips on the taximeter.
** Increases the size of Bolt Driver app, and also future integrations will require added SDKs to Bolt Driver app.

*Option 2: On-Device Application (Leveraging X-One)*

* *Architecture:* (This assumes the taximeter system uses or is integrated into a Digitax X-One Android device which has independent internet connectivity).
** A dedicated application is developed and installed directly onto the Digitax X-One device.
** This application uses the _internal_ Digitax SDK/APIs ({{X-One_Android_System_Features_R1.4.pdf}}, {{AITP functionalities.pdf}}) to communicate with the taximeter function/AITP.
** This application connects directly to the Bolt Backend over the X-One's own internet connection (SIM/Wi-Fi).
** The Bolt Backend sends commands to this application, which controls the taximeter.
** The Bolt Driver App on the driver's separate phone may not need to be involved in taximeter communication at all, or only for displaying information relayed via the backend.
* *Pros:*
** Potentially eliminates the need for the driver's _personal_ phone/Bolt Driver app to handle the taximeter connection.
** Leverages the capabilities of the existing Digitax hardware.
** Allows direct backend control.
* *Cons:*
** Highly dependent on the capabilities, openness, and internet connectivity of the specific Digitax X-One device model used.
** Requires developing a specific application tailored to the Digitax X-One Android environment.
** Requires managing the deployment and updates of this application on the X-One devices.
** Feasibility needs verification – can custom background applications be reliably run? Does it have persistent internet? Can it access the necessary taximeter APIs/SDK functions?
** New App should be compatible with Android 7 (double-check the version on device)

~ Summary of Events ~

Aditya Mony, a resident of India, reported that his email address ([amony@yahoo.com|mailto:amony@yahoo.com]) was being erroneously linked to a Bolt customer account belonging to Mona Mohammed Fehaid AL-Marri (Account No: 35865018) in Saudi Arabia. He stated that he has never used the Bolt app or created an account, yet continues to receive Bolt communications, including trip receipts. Despite Bolt confirming at one point that his email was removed from their system, the emails continued, indicating that his personal data was still being processed without consent.

Aditya first reported the issue to [privacy@bolt.eu|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu] on July 12, 2024, and escalated it on July 15 due to lack of resolution. On December 9, 2024, he escalated further to [help@bolt.eu|mailto:help@bolt.eu] and [privacy@bolt.eu|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu]. On December 11, he received a confirmation that his email had been removed and that no further unsolicited emails would be sent. However, on December 31, Bolt contradicted this by stating that there was no account linked to his email. On January 2, 2025, Aditya reported continued emails and received a message from Bolt asking for clarification and acknowledging that he had previously been told his email was removed.

An internal investigation revealed that while the account email had been corrected in December, the complainant’s email remained in the user’s “Work Profile,” a separate feature not linked to the main account email. This allowed emails to continue being sent despite the account correction. Engineers ultimately updated the work profile email to resolve the issue.

In closing, the matter was addressed. On 21st February, the data subject was informed that her email address was removed from both the user and work profiles, and it was also added, on February 13, to a new internal blocklist reporting tool designed to prevent it from being linked to other profiles in the future. Bolt also provided a formal response to AKI on February 26, acknowledging Aditya Mony’s GDPR complaint and explaining how the Work Profile feature functions, the nature of the issue, the steps taken to resolve it, and how the new blocklist feature mitigates the risk of recurrence. The response was translated by NJORD and sent to AKI.

# Find the last merged PR, skipping the automated deployment PRs raised by {{botblot}} (similar logic to {{builder_ci/common/check_pr.jenkinsfile}}).

# From this point on, proceed as a regular pipeline.

*Data Breach type:* Breach of Confidentiality

*Breach description:* Gmail can assign two unrelated conversations to the same thread if they begin with very similar email messages – such as the invoices Bolt sends after completed rides. BH is based on the Gmail system. Two customers may be communicating with the same agent through one support case.

* Identified 30 cases that could have been affected from last week: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1lVkehtExCTjDcNmdx-BvkWH2AAPZBeAGu3igR16NrDU/edit?gid=0#gid=0|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1lVkehtExCTjDcNmdx-BvkWH2AAPZBeAGu3igR16NrDU/edit?gid=0#gid=0|smart-link] 
* Incident may have started in November 2024
* There could have been approximately 1500 messages with the bug since the start of the incident and fix

*Mitigating measures:* Bug was fixed

* We create separate support cases if we receive messages from different email addresses, even if Gmail stores them under a single thread



{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Problematic cases*

When Gmail incorrectly merges unrelated messages into the same thread, our system may create *separate support cases* for each message — one for each sender. However, due to how Beehive handles threading, *all replies in that thread are sent to the original sender in the Gmail thread*, regardless of which case the agent is responding from — causing the agent to believe all messages are from that same person.

{color:#bf2600}*High risk:*{color} If CS agent is unknowingly communicating with two different users and one of them requests access to personal information, CS may send or share the data to the incorrect person. CS may also perform changes on the request of one User on other User’s account.
{panel}



*Analyzed all the Problematic Treads provided so far (as of EOD 31.03.2025):* 

* No personal data shared with unauthorized party detected

+*CONTENTS OF MARKETING EMAILS*+

* Identity of sender:
** PECR requires identity of the sender to be clear in marketing comms. Recipient should clearly understand who is contacting them.
*** This does not necessarily need to amount to a full legal name. Using a trading name that is well-known to the recipient should be sufficient.
*** Issues only arise where there are multiple entities operating under similar trading names.
** As such, specifying that ‘Bolt’ is sending the comms may well be enough.
*** Indeed, this is the approach that will be taken (see [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FkEe0FLwWYvbWoFqbeZW5rqn6sSch22O0CJ9buvLn9o/edit?tab=t.0]): “_We are not mentioning entities in the comms at all. From our initial discussion, not a lot of things are changing in terms of user experience. Bolt is still Bolt. It would be ideal not to add this in our comms moving forward since the user can switch frequently between one model vs another so this will cause gaps in targeting that can result in users receiving comms from one entity when they are in the other._”
*** I should {color:#4c9aff}*take a look at current marketing comms*{color} for level of granularity.
** Nevertheless, current plan is for comms to come from different email addresses, with a separate entity listed in the email footer (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08GT6EUS23/p1745483399723959]).
* Link to privacy notice:
** No need to include privacy notice links in marketing emails. Already provided upon registration, and when a user clicks the ‘unsubscribe’ option in a marketing email they are directed to the unsubscribe web page, which contains a link to the privacy notice (see Kost discussion [+here+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D07AFGZ3V6F/p1744792265966109]).

h2. Updates regarding the delayed deletion of the user accounts

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Design doc for* [+*deferred deletion of user accounts*+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/5586911788/2025-03+Deferred+deletion+of+user+accounts+Design+doc] - Privacy Team final analysis addressed to [~accountid:712020:1ebf0171-ae70-4b79-bb86-c9b52209b3dd] 
{panel}

# *Communication:* We should ensure that any marketing or other comms (except the ones related to the account deletion) are not sent to the user when they requested the account deletion. As users will have a right to access the app within 20 days from the request, but not making orders (soft-blocking), we need to ensure no pop-ups, notifications, emails, or other information are sent to such users.
# *Cancelation link and other comms related to account deletion - verified and not verified emails:* After the clarification, we will send a cancelation link and deletion emails to both verified and not verified emails. This raises some concerns as to the privacy of users.
## As an alternative, can we show a pop-up in the app to the accounts with unverified emails before the deletion, asking them to verify their email before the deletion is possible? As we send the cancelation link to emails, such a request complies with the law to ensure the cancelation link is not sent to not an owner of the account.
## Main concerns here that the original requestor will not receive emails related to deletions as they may be addressed to another email, another user may cancel the deletion request, or will have access to these deletion emails. It may also trigger these users making requests to Bolt that their email is re-used.
# *Requesting exports in the app within a soft-block:* Until an account is deleted (and even after) users have a right to request their data. If they make this request to the CS, we would unlikely satisfy their request within 20 days due to internal processes and it may lead to non-compliance. If we leave this option in the app for at least 16-18 days before deletion, we will show that we give this opportunity to users and satisfy their requests.
## [~accountid:712020:1ebf0171-ae70-4b79-bb86-c9b52209b3dd]  will it take a lot of efforts to make sure we give this option?
# *Deletion email:* Can we also send the email to the user on the day when the account was deleted? We need to inform users about the outcome of the deletion under the GDPR. Additionally, as we send this request to both verified and not verified emails, it may be a case that someone may cancel the deletion request.

# Issuing a pre-bill to the customer: The waiter issues a pre-bill for the full order amount. This pre-bill is handed to the customer. 
# Paying via the app: The customer then opens the Bolt Food app and enters the full order amount shown on the pre-bill. Upon a payment customer gets cashback credit to his Bolt Balance and receives a code in an app confirming the payment.
# Recording the sale in the restaurant's POS: The waiter checks from Bolt Waiter App whether payment is received based on the code/ID provided by the customer. One problem we noticed during the upgrade is that Elastic Beanstalk manages the permissions of the bucket used for storing the zip files with the application code ({{elasticbeanstalk-eu-central-1-655979121739}}) in prelive. When destroying an environment, it adds an invalid principal to the policy that looks like this (the last line):

{code:json}"AWS": [
	"arn:aws:iam::655979121739:role/bolt-pci-payments-prelive-eu-central-1-eb-ec2",
	"arn:aws:iam::655979121739:role/bolt-pci-payments-silent-prelive-eu-central-1-eb-ec2",
	"arn:aws:iam::655979121739:role/bolt-pci-payments-private-prelive-eu-central-1-eb-ec2",
	"AROAZRO3HBRFTBKYF6ZHM"
]{code}



This caused an error about a malformed bucket policy when redeploying the bucket. I’m assuming its because beanstalk tries parsing the policy again to add the new principal upon creating an environment, however the parsing step fails.

The fix was to remove the invalid principal from the bucket policy manually.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*You have approval to collect personal data from Fleet Partner Personnel (Managing Director, UBOs, Senior Management/Representative). However, you must ensure that we only collect personal data that is* +*necessary*+ *to achieve the purpose here (complying with KYC/AML screening obligations).*
{panel}

# *No consent is required.*

* In Taiwan we are entitled to collect personal data from these persons if _expressly required by law_, without consent. In Taiwan the following law/regulation imposes obligations on Bolt to collect this personal data:
** [+Regulation governing AML and CTF for TPPSP+|https://law.moj.gov.tw/ENG/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=J0080060]
** [+Guidelines governing AML/CTF for TPPSP+|https://www-api.moda.gov.tw/File/Get/adi/zh-tw/de34Wd9NEQ7iipw]

{quote}Based on [+Regulations governing AML/CTF for TPPSP+|https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=J0080060]: *_latest amendment on 29 Nov 2024 (please don't directly click on the English version of the regulation on the website which has not yet reflected the latest amendment; please use direct google translation on the Chinese version)_*

* *Para 3 Article 7*: When the client is a legal person, group or trust, the client’s business nature and its *actual beneficiary* should be understood, and relevant information should be obtained in accordance with the provisions of this Department in order to verify the identity of the client and its actual beneficiary.
* *Article 8:* When confirming the identity of a customer, third-party payment service providers should politely refuse to establish a business relationship or provide services if any of the following circumstances occur:
* *Article 11*: When confirming the identity of a customer, third-party payment service providers should ask the customer and use external databases or information sources to confirm whether *the customer or its senior management personnel* are currently or have been in important political positions in domestic or foreign governments or international organizations, and handle it in accordance with the following regulations:

Based on the [+Guideline governing AML/CTF for TPPSP+|https://www-api.moda.gov.tw/File/Get/adi/zh-tw/de34Wd9NEQ7iipw]:

* *Question 5 of Section 2 (Q&A):* Explain the definition of ultimate beneficial owners (UBO). Please note that based on global standard, holding more 25% of the company ownership will be considered as UBO. (Page 7)
* *Question 6 of Section 2 (Q&A)*: Explain the scope of senior management including directors, general manager, CFO, finance/accounting supervisor or anyone who can act or make decision on behalf of the company. (Page 7)
* *AML/CTF Internal Control Template:* (Page 21 to Page 40)
** Identification of ultimate beneficial owner (Page 24)
** Identification of senior management (Page 30): If the senior management is considered as Politically Exposed Person (PEP), then the customers may need to be rated as High risk depending on the influence of the senior management over the company{quote}

# *No Privacy Notice/Disclosures are required.* 

* In Taiwan [+Article 8 of the PDPA+|https://law.moj.gov.tw/Eng/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?media=print&pcode=I0050021#:~:text=Government%20or%20non%2Dgovernment%20agencies%20shall%20expressly%20inform%20the%20data%20subject%20of%20the%20following%20information%20when%20colleting%20their%20personal%20data%20in%20accordance%20with%20Article%2015%20or%2019%20of%20the%20PDPA%3A] requires Bolt to 'Notify' data subjects about specific information when collecting their personal data (usually in the form of a Privacy Notice). *However, it seems that the PDPA in Taiwan includes an exception* "_where the collection of personal data is necessary for....._ {{the non-government agencies to fulfill their statutory obligation}}.
* However, we still recommend letting Fleet Personnel know, in the Form that they provide their information, that “_Please note that Bolt is required by law to collect this personal data and it will be used for KYC and AML purposes_. _Your personal data will be processed in accordance with the Personal Data Protection Act, 2023”_.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*As I mentioned on the last Weekly MODA Call, it is very important to keep in mind that if we go beyond what we are required to collect by law, we can no longer rely on the relevant exception under Taiwan’s Data Protection Law. Therefore, please double check what personal data we are asking from these persons and verify it against* [+Regulation governing AML and CTF for TPPSP+|https://law.moj.gov.tw/ENG/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=J0080060] +and+ [+Guidelines governing AML/CTF for TPPSP+|https://www-api.moda.gov.tw/File/Get/adi/zh-tw/de34Wd9NEQ7iipw]+.+

Hi [~accountid:712020:29d8b602-d17f-40cd-9cae-5653bc2c54b7] 

There is no difference between the regular payout and Early Cashouts in terms of the payout process. In Canada, the account owner and the account recipient will be the same. From the point of view of invoicing, everything will look the same as well.

The only difference is that the regular payouts are made once per week on Monday morning and the Early Cashouts may be requested by the driver at any moment of time. So, there indeed may be a situation when the driver requests funds that have not been settled by the card acquirer to our bank account yet. For these cases we allocate a liquidity buffer to the bank account equal to ~3 business days of average Early Cashout volume in a given market (this amount may vary depending on the situation). 

I suppose, in Canada we will have to agree with Airwallex how to provide the liquidity buffer for the Early Cashouts (or use some kind of overdraft). Normally, in the “developed” markets the Cashout share (i. e. the % of the earnings the drivers prefer to receive via Early Cashoust vs regular payouts) does not exceed 30%, so this feature does not create liquidity issues. The concrete solution is TBD. 

If you have any other questions, I will be happy to help.

Based on this agreement, *with the exclusion of the cross border rides (see below)*, the Client will be able also to ride within the borders of any other country which offers Bolt services. In case of riding Bolt in any other country, the local T&C will apply.
Please be informed however, that according to the Polish law and our local T&Cs, the Client’s employees cannot take up any cross border ride, i.e., any ride that started in Poland and, at any time, crossed the border of Poland.
According to the Polish transport law, Bolt drivers in Poland are performing their services based on the license to carry passengers. This license is granted only for the territory of Poland. This means, that the Bolt drivers in Poland cannot cross the border with the passenger on board. According to Bolt’s T&Cs, Bolt will cancel an order which destination exceeds the territory for which the license was granted.

Hi! As for the legal assessment for *Sweden,* also separately aligned with [@lina.dahlander|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U03FG3JENUV], *we can proceed with disabling email receipts, without updating our T&Cs for now, if business wishes to*, based on the following:

* *T&Cs overview*: Our terms state _"Receipts are sent to the email address provided in your profile."_ Changing this require a formal update to the T&Cs, customer notification and a 15-day notice period before the new terms take effect (which I understand we do not have time for now).
* *Legal requirements*: Email receipts are not legally required but are the market standard to reduce customer complaints.
* *Durable medium requirement*: Receipts must be accessible over time and storing receipts only in an app carries risks (e.g., account deletion), so email remains a safer alternative.
* *Consumer protection risks*: Disabling email receipts could pose risks to consumer protection. If complaints arise or authorities review the practice, there could be consequences including that the new practice is deemed invalid, potential reversion to old terms, regulatory scrutiny, liability (should a consumer face financial loss as a consequence) and reputational damage.

*However, given the business-critical nature and presumably low risk of consumers complaining, we can proceed with this without updating our T&Cs at this stage, even though it's not ideal from a consumer protection perspective.*

Hey [~accountid:5dc535abb8eb490c677a579c] mainly this is a step to start sender reputation handling from our end. Currently we have no email address validation, we do nothing with inboxes who bounce as {{quota reached}} (full inbox – can’t accept emails) or {{invalid addresses}}. Even though after 3 soft bounces that email address turns into a hard bounce and then the {{is_undeliverable_email}} property logic kicks in, we still harm our reputation in the meantime with soft bounces that could be prevented.

The poor habits of ours as a sender + poor list hygiene puts us on various DNS Blocklists, then even more (or for example all emails) start to bounce and this turns into never ending story of us being blocked > not delivering autocomms > reaching out to the blacklists to plea for de-listing > they usually give us best practices what to fix on our end > we do nothing > get listed again 😅

Here’s some logged cases from the start of the year where we have been blocked due to reputation [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MLC-713?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiYTYyMjExNjRmZjNjNDFlY2EwNDJmOTljMjk5YTc4YmIiLCJwIjoiaiJ9|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MLC-713?atlOrigin=eyJpIjoiYTYyMjExNjRmZjNjNDFlY2EwNDJmOTljMjk5YTc4YmIiLCJwIjoiaiJ9|smart-link] 

Most recent one (not listed separately as sub task in the epic yet), from March 10th to March 24th got all of our autocomms (regardless of vertical) blocked by [icloud.com|http://icloud.com] so we delivered nothing to those users for couple weeks – this while not much in terms of affected userbase, still was around 10M mark of email volume per week.

Recommendations from icloud Postmaster are the following:

# Review and clean email sending list, ensuring emails are sent only to valid addresses with confirmed opt-ins or recent engagement.
# Reduce email volume to iCloud and focus on sending to highly engaged recipients—specifically those engaging via email, not just an app or website.
# Implement double opt-in if not already in place.
# Strengthening sunset policy to remove unengaged recipients.
# Since iCloud (and Gmail) do not report spam complaints, it would be beneficial to proactively manage engagement to avoid further reputation issues.

It would help with starting to build logic in Braze to skip email sends if user email bounced due to being invalid, dormant, organisation policy, etc. and keep those users only on Push/In-app comms combination. At the same time, vertical teams would be able to create evergreen automations via non-email channels to ask users to proactively update their contact information to correct one.

(a) reasonable segregation of environment
(b) segregation of secrets and connections

The easiest way is create new site from {{airflow-main}} repo (Most recommended). We had some examples  from commerce and geo.
1. [https://github.com/bolteu/airflow-main/tree/main/dags/commerce|https://github.com/bolteu/airflow-main/tree/main/dags/commerce|smart-link] 
2. [https://github.com/bolteu/airflow-main/tree/main/dags/geo|https://github.com/bolteu/airflow-main/tree/main/dags/geo|smart-link]  

They have segregation of environment, segregation of secrets and connections, and allowing flexibility in dependencies, logic, and code, changes. 

You can easily achieve the goal without create other repo. 

For the follow-up answers:

# This is the submodule technique. Deployment, and CI/CD will be used from {{airflow-main}} repo. You will not have isolated k8s cluster and CI/CD, you only have separated code. However, maintaining submodule to running in the same environment and standard is also not an easy task. You need to back and forth between new repo and {{airflow-main}} repo to see how is the deployment and CI going (other toil). We also need to research it to do it in DAP first.

# If infra sits in DAP ownership, i would recommend  {{airflow-main}} repo or submodule technique.

If DAP cannot access the cluster due security concern, your team need to do the same work as DAP do. It’s reasonably doable with extra operation efforts. It’s already happened for secret project because of NDA, we just set it up and they maintain it by themselves.  They chose to use [https://aws.amazon.com/managed-workflows-for-apache-airflow/|https://aws.amazon.com/managed-workflows-for-apache-airflow/|smart-link]  instead use separated airflow code. It makes the management of airflow still manageable.

But If you don’t want to use MWAA and have same infra as {{airflow-main}} repo (in-house k8s, runner, libraries, etc), your team need to keep watch all infra related, security related, update related, monitoring the infra and DAG, etc.

# The previous setup for {{previous-isolated-project}} databricks is 2 weeks effort without CI/CD. Isolated infra will take more than 2 weeks since we need to research it too. However, we had our prioritization too, we cannot jump to it for this week directly since it’s big project.

# *Conducts invoked on the complaint by the costumer:*

* Crime de “fraude informática” e burla (art. 221.º e 217.º do Código Penal) já que, alegadamente, nenhuma das empresas está legalmente constituída. (Não existe nenhum crime intitulado fraude informática mas sim burla informática). +Burla informática+: _Quem, com intenção de obter para si ou para terceiro enriquecimento ilegítimo, causar a outra pessoa prejuízo patrimonial, mediante interferência no resultado de tratamento de dados, estruturação incorreta de programa informático, utilização incorreta ou incompleta de dados, utilização de dados sem autorização ou intervenção por qualquer outro modo não autorizada no processamento, é punido com pena de prisão até 3 anos ou com pena de multa._ +Burla+: _Quem, com intenção de obter para si ou para terceiro enriquecimento ilegítimo, por meio de erro ou engano sobre factos que astuciosamente provocou, determinar outrem à prática de actos que lhe causem, ou causem a outra pessoa, prejuízo patrimonial é punido com pena de prisão até três anos ou com pena de multa._ +O reclamante+ +acha que configura burla por induzir em erro os consumidores sobre a origem dos serviços e a burla informática por manipulação de dados informáticos para obter vantagem ilegítima.+
* Concorrência desleal, sendo que é mencionada a Lei n.º 19/2012, que não tem qualquer definição de concorrência desleal no artigo 5.º. A Lei correta neste caso é o Código de Propriedade Industrial, nomeadamente o artigo 311.º: Constitui concorrência desleal todo o ato de concorrência contrário às normas e usos honestos de qualquer ramo de atividade económica, nomeadamente: a) Os atos suscetíveis de criar confusão com a empresa, o estabelecimento, os produtos ou os serviços dos concorrentes, qualquer que seja o meio empregue; b) As falsas afirmações feitas no exercício de uma atividade económica, com o fim de desacreditar os concorrentes; c) As invocações ou referências não autorizadas feitas com o fim de beneficiar do crédito ou da reputação de um nome, estabelecimento ou marca alheios; d) As falsas indicações de crédito ou reputação próprios, respeitantes ao capital ou situação financeira da empresa ou estabelecimento, à natureza ou âmbito das suas atividades e negócios e à qualidade ou quantidade da clientela; e) As falsas descrições ou indicações sobre a natureza, qualidade ou utilidade dos produtos ou serviços, bem como as falsas indicações de proveniência, de localidade, região ou território, de fábrica, oficina, propriedade ou estabelecimento, seja qual for o modo adotado; f) A supressão, ocultação ou alteração, por parte do vendedor ou de qualquer intermediário, da denominação de origem ou indicação geográfica dos produtos ou da marca registada do produtor ou fabricante em produtos destinados à venda e que não tenham sofrido modificação no seu acondicionamento. +Dizem que ocorre uma exploração indevida de reputação já que nomes como "Premium Sushi Lounge" sugerem qualidade não verificada.+ 
* Lei do Cibercrime - o conceito invocado na denúncia de “abuso de sistemas informáticos“ não existe na Lei do Cibercrime.
* Artigo 5.º do RGPD. Princípio da exatidão no tratamento de dados pessoais. Os dados pessoais são exatos e atualizados sempre que necessário; devem ser adotadas todas as medidas adequadas para que os dados inexatos, tendo em conta as finalidades para que são tratados, sejam apagados ou retificados sem demora. Caso se verifique incumprimento deste princípio, o responsável pelo tratamento pratica uma contraordenação muito grave (artigo 83.º, n.º 5, alínea a) RGPD).
* Publicidade enganosa. +Os consumidores são induzidos em erro, acreditando tratar-se de estabelecimentos distintos, quando todos os pedidos são preparados no mesmo local,+ +_sem condições higiénicas adequadas_++.+

# *Conducts invoked on the complaint by the costumer:*

* Crime of “computer fraud” and swindling (art. 221 and 217 of the Penal Code) since, allegedly, none of the companies are legally incorporated. (There is no crime entitled computer fraud but rather computer swindling). +Computer fraud+: _Anyone who, with the intention of obtaining unlawful enrichment for themselves or a third party, causes another person to suffer pecuniary loss by interfering with the result of data processing, incorrectly structuring a computer program, incorrect or incomplete use of data, use of data without authorization or otherwise unauthorized intervention in the processing, is punished with imprisonment for up to 3 years or a fine._ +Fraud+: _Anyone who, with the intention of obtaining unlawful enrichment for themselves or for a third party, by means of error or deception about facts which they have cunningly caused, causes another person to perform acts which cause them, or another person, pecuniary damage, shall be punished with imprisonment of up to three years or a fine._ +The complainant+ +believes that this constitutes fraud by misleading consumers about the origin of the services and computer fraud by manipulating computer data to obtain an illegitimate advantage.+
* Unfair competition, as Law 19/2012 is mentioned, which has no definition of unfair competition in Article 5. The correct law in this case is the Industrial Property Code, specifically Article 311: Any act of competition contrary to the rules and honest uses of any branch of economic activity constitutes unfair competition, namely: a) Acts likely to create confusion with the company, establishment, products or services of competitors, whatever the means employed; b) False statements made in the exercise of an economic activity, with the aim of discrediting competitors; c) Unauthorized invocations or references made in order to benefit from the credit or reputation of another's name, establishment or brand; d) False indications of one's own credit or reputation, concerning the capital or financial situation of the company or establishment, the nature or scope of its activities and business and the quality or quantity of its clientele; e) False descriptions or indications of the nature, quality or usefulness of products or services, as well as false indications of provenance, locality, region or territory, factory, workshop, property or establishment, in any way whatsoever; f) The suppression, concealment or alteration, by the seller or any intermediary, of the designation of origin or geographical indication of the products or the registered trademark of the producer or manufacturer on products intended for sale and which have not undergone any modification in their packaging. +They say there is an undue exploitation of reputation since names like “Premium Sushi Lounge” suggest unverified quality.+
* Cybercrime Law - the concept invoked in the complaint of “abuse of computer systems” does not exist in the Cybercrime Law.
* Article 5 of the GDPR. Principle of accuracy in the processing of personal data. Personal data shall be accurate and kept up to date whenever necessary; all appropriate measures shall be taken to ensure that inaccurate data, taking into account the purposes for which it is processed, is erased or rectified without delay. If this principle is not complied with, the controller commits a very serious offense (Article 83(5)(a) GDPR).
* Misleading advertising. +Consumers are misled into believing that these are different establishments, when all orders are prepared in the same place,+ +_without adequate hygienic conditions_++.+

# *Sanctions invoked on the complaint (all the articles that are invoked are not right.* *However, the DLs alleged are applicable)* DL n.º 7/2004, de 7 de janeiro (Electronic commerce in the internal market and processing of personal data). An important DL for assessing Bolt's liability.

* Another major objective of the directive is to determine the liability regime for intermediary service providers.
* The regulatory authority for Bolt is not ASAE but ANACOM (article 35, no. 2 DL no. 7/2004).
* Duties to be complied with by Bolt - if it becomes aware of illegal conduct by partners: _Article 13_
* _Common duties of intermediary service providers_
* _Intermediary service providers are under an obligation to the competent authorities:_
* _a) To inform immediately when they become aware of illegal activities carried out through the services they provide;_
* Failure by Bolt to comply with the above-mentioned article 13 gives rise to a fine (according to article 37, no. 2, point c) from €5,000.00 to 100,000.00) increased by 1/3 in the minimum and maximum limits due to the fact that Bolt is a legal person. There is also the possibility of an accessory sanction being applied, in accordance with the provisions of article 38, no. 2 of Decree-Law no. 7/2004, of January 7.

User flagged that the email address is [seychellco@hotmail.com|mailto:seychellco@hotmail.com] and the phone number is +346 99121261.

Hi [~accountid:712020:1a3a17cb-2e37-4162-8d95-4d1059255d7e] , thanks for looping me in. Here’s my input from a privacy perspective:

* *Fleet owner data* is generally *not considered personal data* when the fleet is operating as a business (e.g. a registered company). In those cases, contact details provided (like a company email or phone number) aren’t protected under GDPR or other privacy laws.
* However, if the *fleet owner is a natural person* (i.e. not operating as a registered company), we should treat their data with more care. Still, in the context of *insurance claims and safety-related cases*, we have a valid *legal basis to share limited information*, especially if it's necessary to resolve the issue and in the interest of the affected rider.
* *What I recommend*:
** Share only the *fleet owner's contact information* (e.g. company name or email address), *not the driver’s data*.
** Keep the shared data *minimal and relevant* to the case.

Lastly, Bolt typically won’t be able to resolve these insurance cases on its own, so some level of data sharing is necessary to support resolution.

Let me know if you need further clarification or input.

Hi [~accountid:5e620d95ed743a0afe39736b] ,

Thanks for submitting this request. From a privacy perspective, if we are talking about customer data (riders), any transfer of personal data must have:

* A clear purpose for the transfer
* An explanation of how the data will be used
* A valid legal basis for processing

There are two main things we need to align on:

# *Data sharing between Bolt and Viggo*
We discussed this with the team before, but to move forward, we need to have a data sharing agreement in place. I am attaching our [*standard template*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1GYNMaJu34OqHTmrPHaCGXkuj7svXtIbopkk0UiWSl8w/edit?tab=t.0]. It is designed for use between two independent service providers, like Bolt and Viggo.

The only thing needed is to complete Annex 1 with the types of data being shared and the purposes. *Please let me know if you can review this or if someone else from your team should handle it.*

# *Transferring customer data from Viggo to Bolt*
This part is more sensitive. A few points to consider:

* If the data was collected under Viggo’s terms and conditions, we cannot assume we have a legal basis to process it ourselves.
* Much of this data was likely collected under the legal basis of performing a contract with Viggo, so it cannot be transferred without consent.
* Sharing data like ride history or using it for marketing purposes would be difficult to justify unless users have clearly agreed.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*_Here are three options to consider, from lowest to highest risk:_*
{panel}

*Option 1: Ask users to join Bolt directly*
Encourage users via pop-ups or messages in the Viggo app to register with Bolt, for example: "Viggo will be phased out soon. To continue riding, please download the Bolt app."

*Option 2: Ask users for consent to transfer their data*
Show a pop-up in the Viggo app explaining what data would be transferred and why. If users agree, then the transfer can be done lawfully. If users disagree or don’t do anything, we don’t transfer their data and delete it (if possible).

*Option 3: Automatically transfer user data*
This is the most risky option. Without a legal basis or user consent, this approach could lead to privacy complaints or regulatory issues. We recommend avoiding this path unless there is a strong justification and clear documentation.

*_Final note_*: It is important to be transparent about what we are doing. Lack of transparency is one of the most common reasons for complaints and regulatory attention. Given the current situation with Viggo, it is especially important to handle this carefully.

Let me know how you would like to proceed or if you have any questions.

Hi Deb 

Following our discussion earlier today, I have discussed the tech fee with my team in more detail and also looked at your comments in the T&Cs. 

As Ieva outlined below on the ticket, Bolt has four options:

# {color:#0747a6}*No Cash Rides in Ireland*{color}{color:#0747a6}: {color}This is the safest option from a legal standpoint, but we understand that it’s not commercially viable given the GMV impact and our competitive advantage over Uber.



# {color:#0747a6}*Tech Fee on Card Payments Only*{color}{color:#0747a6}:{color} This carries both regulatory and contractual risks, (as flagged by [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba])



# {color:#0747a6}*Tech Fee on All Rides (Cash & Card)*{color}{color:#0747a6}:{color} This is not viable as the National Transport Authority (NTA ) prohibits charging a tech fee on cash rides. [~accountid:610279859798100070592384] has confirmed that the NTA would strongly oppose this.

[~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba] To address your question, charging this on cash rides presents a higher risk because the NTA, the regulator responsible for regulating public transport, including taxis, hackneys, and limousines. As Deb mentioned below they oversee the pricing structure. Therefore, if Bolt were found to be in violation of these rules, it could lead to significant regulatory issues.



# {color:#0747a6} {color}{color:#0747a6}*Tech Fee on Card Payments & Account Charging for Cash Rides*{color}{color:#0747a6}: {color}While the surcharge risk here is lower than Option 2, there is still a surcharge risk. Even if our T&Cs state that the tech fee is applied as an account charge, regulators (such as the CCPC) will focus on how we operate in practice rather than just what’s written in the terms. That said, our current draft T&Cs allow for this option.

As highlighted by Ieva, Options 2 and 4 appear to be the only viable options. Ultimately, none of these options (except Option 1, which we’ve ruled out) are entirely risk free - it’s a matter of whether the business is comfortable assuming the associated risks.

{color:#0747a6}*Terms and Conditions, outlining the amount £*{color}: External counsel advised that the surcharge risk is {color:#ff5630}+*high*+{color}, but mitigation measures (including clear and transparent wording in our terms and conditions) can reduce it to {color:#ff991f}+*medium*+{color}. While we appreciate competitors may keep their fees vague, our recommendation is to maintain a flat fee to avoid increasing the risk further. If the business prefers more flexibility in wording, you’d need to be comfortable assuming that additional risk.

{color:#0747a6}*Updating the terms and conditions:*{color}{color:#0747a6} {color}We’re also waiting on final confirmation from accounting regarding payment localisation timing (currently looking at month-end or a Monday). Legal can finalise the T&Cs and liaise with the Marketing Team to send notifications out once we align on a date. 

However, I’d suggest confirming the tech fee approach first, as including wording that later becomes irrelevant wouldn’t be ideal. 

Alternatively, we could proceed with updating the T&Cs now to cover Early Cash Out and the Fraud Policy, and revisit the tech fee once a decision has been made on the approach/launch moving forward. 

Happy to discuss all the above and any other queries tomorrow on our call.

Many thanks for the summary [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3], really appreciate it. 

Just to clarify, it is not that the NTA have ruled out an additional charge on cash fees _per se_, it is just that they take their role in setting fares very seriously, and any attempt to require/ induce drivers to become involved in any top ups/ changes to the fare would be deemed to breach their legislation. If we want to directly charge passengers for using our platform, the NTA can’t stop us, but we are not allowed involve our drivers in the process or require them to add on any extra charges to the direct fare, which is what we feared would occur if the fee was applied to cash trips. 

The outcome is the same as summarised above by Anusha, just though tit would be helpful to understand the rationale for the NTA’s opposition to the fee on cash trips.

hey [~accountid:62b1c880566f3e7b0a8f2eb7] - no, we don’t require all couriers to buy a bag. They do need to use one, but they don’t have to purchase a new one, especially one branded with Bolt Food logo.  But tbh, not a huge fan of this approach:

# Reclass side - requiring couriers to work with out branded equipment is a pretty big issue. 
# Operational side - this approach suggests that buying a bag will mean you will get “accepted” as a courier. This might not be the case. This can lead to disputes and is not good PR. And not sure how it works in UA, but before the courier signs up on our platform as a business user, they are probably protected by consumer rights/ unfair commercial practices. 
# Overall “platform” narrative - if we want to argue that we are simply a delivery platform, then our role as a platform should be limited to making sure the couriers who sign up have the required documents, and that’s it. Requiring them to basically pay for the possibility to sign up (without guaranteeing “acceptance”) is imo problematic. Also ties into reclass topic (i.e. can we be seen as controlling onboarding/access to work).
# Not sure of the marketshare / competition law issues in UA, but if we are a dominant player, then this rings some bells from the competition law side as well - we are requiring them to purchase a new bag (even if they already have one?), effectively tying the access to one product/service to buying another product. Would not be ok in EU, especially with a big marketshare.

h3. *How Google reCAPTCHA Functions*
{panel}

* *Advanced Analysis:* Google reCAPTCHA utilizes cutting-edge AI and machine learning technologies to perform risk analyses based on user behavior, device details, IP addresses, and various other signals. This analysis helps ascertain whether a website visitor is a genuine user or an automated bot.
* *Invisible Mode:* One of the standout features of reCAPTCHA is its invisible functionality. This means it operates in the background without interrupting or delaying the user experience by asking them to solve puzzles. Only in cases where the AI cannot definitively identify a user as human, it will prompt them with a challenge.
* *Security Measures:* Although highly effective at enhancing security, no system is entirely foolproof. Advanced bots and CAPTCHA-solving services can sometimes bypass reCAPTCHA. Nonetheless, it remains a solid barrier against the vast majority of automated attacks.



{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
h3. *Google reCAPTCHA v2:*
{panel}

* *User Interaction:* Requires direct interaction from users, commonly known as the "I am not a robot" checkbox. Users might also be asked to solve image-based puzzles if further verification is needed.
* *Visibility:* It's always visible and requires user action to proceed, which can occasionally disrupt the user experience but verify active participation in the verification process.
* *Implementation:* It’s straightforward and offers a clear indication that a security measure is in place, which can be reassuring for users but also a potential annoyance.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
h3. *Google reCAPTCHA v3:*
{panel}

* *User Interaction:* Operates completely in the background, analyzing user behavior without any required interaction. Users do not need to check boxes or solve puzzles.
* *Visibility:* Invisible to users, providing a seamless experience. It assesses the risk associated with each visitor automatically based on numerous interactions over the course of their visit.
* *Implementation:* More complex due to its background operational nature, but offers a more refined user experience that doesn’t interrupt browsing or shopping activities.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
h3. Data *Google reCAPTCHA* collects
{panel}

* IP address

* Operating system
* Cookies
* Mouse movements and keyboard strokes
* Duration of pauses between actions
* Device settings, such as language or location

h2. *Summary*

Under Romanian law, sending marketing communications requires *valid, prior consent* from both drivers and fleets. Even if a communication is framed as operational, there is a high likelihood that the Romanian regulator would classify it as *marketing* if the content promotes services or commercial offerings.

Therefore, we recommend to obtain *consent for third-party marketing before proceeding*, unless a strong case can be made for the message being purely operational or compliance-related.

----

h2. *Regulatory Risks and Considerations*

* The *safest and most compliant approach* is to treat this communication as *marketing* and collect *opt-in consent* from drivers to share their data with third-party partners for support services.
* The *consent mechanism* must clearly state that data will be shared with third parties.
** We recommend that the *business team draft the initial consent language* for Privacy to review and refine.
* If partners are reaching out to drivers, they can avoid explicitly mentioning Bolt in the initial outreach, and may refer only to the category of the data source (e.g. 'a transportation services partner').
** However, *if a driver contacts Bolt and/or the partner*, they have the right to request the names of the entities with whom their data was shared or from whom it was received (_internal – update from my side, per WP29 guidelines_).
** *Failure by either Bolt or the partner to disclose this information* would constitute a breach of transparency obligations and could trigger regulatory escalation.
* GDPR is a directly applicable EU-wide regulation. Our lead supervisory authority is *AKI in Estonia*, which oversees compliance across all EU operations:
** any complaint or issue raised in Romania could escalate into a *broader EU-wide investigation* around Bolt’s marketing and communication practices. This increases both the *regulatory scope and potential exposure*.
** We are already managing a *high volume of supervisory inquiries*, especially involving marketing communications directed at drivers and riders.

----

h2. *Operational Messaging – Reframing Opportunity*

Given the business's strong interest in exploring an operational communication pathway, we can suggest expanding this avenue with *clear guardrails and risk awareness*:

* It may be possible to *frame certain communications as operational or compliance-related* (rather than promotional), particularly where they relate to changes in Romanian law affecting driver eligibility (e.g., fleet compliance rules from May 1st).
* Messaging of this nature must:
** Focus on *legal compliance* or *driver obligations*, not promote services directly.
** Be *tied to the driver’s status or activity* (e.g., missing documentation or risk of suspension).
** Avoid marketing tone or benefit-driven language.

{quote}*Example script (business input needed):*
_"Hi, we received your data from our partner for the purpose of providing services. We're currently checking how prepared you are for the upcoming changes in Romanian law. As of May 1st, drivers with non-compliant fleets (e.g., missing documents) will be banned from ride-hailing platforms. To avoid any disruption, we’d like to consult with you and suggest moving to a compliant fleet we work with."_{quote}

This type of framing positions the outreach as a *compliance advisory*, not a commercial offer. We recommend *preparing several variations* of these scripts, based on business needs, for Privacy review.

----

h2. *Final Recommendations*

h4. ✅ *Consent-Based Approach* (Preferred)

* Collect valid, specific *opt-in consent* from drivers to share their data with named third-party partners.
* Drivers who do not consent *cannot be contacted* by those partners with messages that can be seen 
* The *business team should propose consent text*, with Privacy support on legal and GDPR-compliant language.

h4. ⚠️ *Bolt-Led Communication (Fallback Option) - High Risk*🔴 

* Frame the message as an *operational update* or *compliance alert*, emphasising the driver’s own situation and legal obligations.

----

h2. *Next Steps*

* Business to confirm preferred approach (consent or operational fallback).
* Draft initial messaging/scripts for the approach.
* Privacy to support with review, compliance check, and final sign-off.

I’ll leave a quick summary of all steps required for upgrading PCI environment versions, for future reference. I’ll mostly use the silent-live env as an example:

* Route all traffic away from environment from the cloudflare load balancer (just disable the pool)
* Create a PR to destroy the environment, so far we have just commented it out - [example|https://github.com/bolteu/pci-beanstalk-infra/pull/288/files]
** Start with your feature branch
** We have separate branches for each environment - silent-prelive, prelive, silent-live, master (live), merge the PR through all of the branches in that exact order. The changes will be applied to the environment you modified when the changes are merged into the corresponding branch. 
** Eventually all changes should be merged to master to enforce consistency through all branches
* The application code is stored in zip files in an s3 bucket - the bucket is managed by elastic beanstalk. By default and in our case all environments in an account use the same bucket. The naming format is like this: {{elasticbeanstalk-eu-central-1-655979121739}}
** *After destroying an environment, we observed that elastic-beanstalk modifies the bucket policy into an invalid format by adding an invalid principal*
** It would replace the role ARN for the destroyed environment with something like this: {{"AROAZRO3HBRFTBKYF6ZHM"}}
** The solution is to remove this invalid principal manually before recreating the environment
** If this step is skipped then upon recreation, elastic beanstalk will throw an error about the malformed bucket policy - I assume in the backend it parses the policy, modifies it and rewrites it into json. The parse step probably fails because of the malformed policy.
* Create a PR to create the environment, just uncomment it - [example|https://github.com/bolteu/pci-beanstalk-infra/pull/291/files]
** The same git flow applies here
* Ask the engineers to deploy their application to the recreated environment
* Once the new version of the application is deployed, you can enable the pool in the load balancer again to start sending traffic to the recreated environment



The process was mostly the same for the private environments. There are currently some extra caveats however. Firstly, we don’t have a solution for doing proper blue/green deployments there. This time we got away with it because it’s not critical yet and we could afford the downtime - no clients were affected.

*For private environments we have an NLB in front of the ALB created by elastic beanstalk. The NLB has the ALB in a target group. This ALB needs to be detached from the target group*. [Example|https://github.com/bolteu/terraform-main/pull/11969/files].

After the private environment has been recreated, get the ARN of the new ALB and attach it to the target group. [Example|https://github.com/bolteu/terraform-main/pull/11970/files].

*Make sure not to mix up the ALB ARNs in this case.*

In simulations we would often see bias. i.e. in simulations the model’s mean does not converge to the true one (see plot).

!Screenshot 2025-04-02 at 11.52.07.png|width=33.333333333333336%,alt="Screenshot 2025-04-02 at 11.52.07.png"!

I tried to decompose the model and make adjustments to find out that:

* *Tourists or seasonal android/ios deviations* do *decrease* the bias, but do not completely eliminate it (we need to control for it)
* Taking out *multicollinearity* (splitting spends) do *decrease* the bias, but do not completely eliminate it.
* Google is often following some wave-pattern (together with demand). Smoothing out Google spend does not eliminate bias (probably decrease, but unobservably small in my examples)
* The bias does not depend on by how much android and ios are different (as long as multiplicative conditions hold)
* Adding the intercept to our models can decrease the model, but not completely eliminates it
* The error that we are modelling does not seem to be multiplicative and therefore assumptions of additive assumptions are not violated.
* There is potentially bias related to the *shape of the curve* (not confirmed). The curve seems to be overpredicting the results more than analogous linear model’s bias (can be due to vmax being in some way attached to total signups (i.e. effect cannot always be more than 20% of signups))
* There can as well be error related to the fact that both android and ios contain random error. This is related to error-in-variance problem. We might instead be using:
** Something like Deming regression (see [here|https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/420459/why-my-deming-regression-line-change-so-much-when-switching-variables-if-they-s])
** Latent variable model (see [here|https://discourse.pymc.io/t/errors-in-variables-model-in-pymc3/3519/2] PyMC specification) (also here’s my attempt to specify [latent variable|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/424278394244957?o=3829506390716583#command/424278394244958])
* (To confirm)There potentially is seasonality between android and ios relations that is not result of ads effect and that we might want to take account of. 

All these potential improvements are listed as part of:

[https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH3-14|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH3-14|smart-link]

* Repetitive trips are seen as _suspicious behaviour_ and we’re allowed to take action based on past events like this to mitigate risk.
* Pre-arranged trips are typically advised against - higher driver/rider matching time, bad for supply. And they’re also seen as suspicious.

However,
* The rider almost never cancels previous trips in order to match with this driver. Driver is just in the right time to pick the rider up - not bad for supply.
* Rider also travels with other drivers.
* Absolutely 0 payment problems for the past 3 months with this matching. 👍 

Especially due to having no payment issues, I don’t see any fraud or bad behaviour here. Just something that we consider suspicious due to frequency of matched orders. And due to the fact that the driver is always close by when rider orders, hints towards the fact that this can still be pre-arranged.

Hi [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] please find below the answer from DTI.

Thanks again for the thoughtful and important questions around privacy, data protection, and compliance. Below is a detailed summary of how Driver Technologies handles data during the pilot program. We prioritize transparency and user trust, and we align with global privacy best practices wherever feasible. We are also FCRA-compliant in the U.S., enabling us to support appropriate use of US driver data for insurance and underwriting purposes where applicable.1. *What personal data are we sharing at this point?*
At this stage of the pilot, *no personal data is being shared by default*.
We may collect and store certain user identifiers, such as *email addresses*, which qualify as personally identifiable information (PII). However, this is not shared with any external party unless:

* Bolt is covering the cost of the Driver app for its drivers, or
* A separate agreement is established for the purchase of anonymized or identifiable data.

When and if data is shared, it is done with clear contractual safeguards and purpose limitations. We do *not* share identifiable video, audio, facial recognition data, or license plates unless explicitly agreed upon and legally authorized.2. *What is the legal basis for the collection and processing of personal data?*
We rely on a combination of:

* *Implied consent*, based on users accepting our privacy policy ([link|https://drivertechnologies.com/privacy-policy/]) and using the app
* *Contractual necessity*, for providing core services
* And, where applicable, *legitimate interest* for certain analytics and safety features

# *If relying on consent, how is it being collected, stored, and can it be withdrawn?*


Consent is not collected via explicit in-app opt-ins. Instead:

* Users are informed of our data practices through our [*privacy policy*|https://drivertechnologies.com/privacy-policy/], which they are required to accept as part of app usage.
* We do *not store individual consent records* (e.g., timestamps or identifiers tied to consent).

At this time, we do not offer an in-app method to withdraw consent. If a user no longer wishes to share data, they must *log out of the app and delete it from their device*.4. *What privacy notices are being provided to drivers?*
We provide a detailed *privacy policy* that:

* Describes what data we collect and why
* Explains how the data is used
* Lists any third parties it may be shared with
* Covers our general retention approach

# *What processes are in place for drivers to exercise their data subject rights (access, deletion, restriction, etc.)?*


Drivers can submit requests via:

* [*A form on our websit*|https://drivertechnologies.com/consumer-report/]*e (*[*link*|https://drivertechnologies.com/consumer-report/]*)*, or
* *Emailing our support or privacy team directly*

We handle these requests manually and in good faith, aligning with privacy principles like data minimization and user control, though we are not certified under any specific regional law.6. *Will any personal data of drivers (e.g., in Paraguay or South Africa) be transferred to the US or other regions?*
Yes. *Some personal data, including email addresses and driving data*, is processed and stored in the *United States*, where our primary infrastructure is located.
We do not transfer data to high-risk jurisdictions such as Russia or China. Where regulatory required, we are fully capable, and have historically stood up localized cloud instances.7. *What safeguards are in place for international transfers?*
At Driver we take commercially reasonable steps to:

* Protect data via *encryption at rest and in transit*
* Limit access to authorized personnel
* Prevent unnecessary exposure of sensitive user data
* We also provide custom obfuscation pipelines ([link|https://driver-gateway.readme.io/reference/sign_in]) to comply with localized privacy laws

# *If SDK integration is pursued post-pilot, will it collect any personal data beyond what’s described in the pilot?*


If SDK integration is added, any new types of data collection will:

* Be documented
* Reflected in updated privacy documentation
* Communicated to both partners and users in advance

There will be *no expansion in data scope* without mutual agreement and disclosure.9. *Data retention – how long are recordings and other personal data stored?*

* *Driving event metadata* is typically retained for *3- 90 days* unless flagged/saved by the user
* *Video/audio recordings* (when collected) are retained for *3–90 days*, unless flagged/saved by the user for incident review or legal purposes
* Anonymized or aggregated data may be retained indefinitely for research and safety analytics

Users may request deletion of their data via email or our website.
Please let us know if you’d like us to provide a current copy of the privacy policy, DPA (if needed), or examples of user-facing disclosures. We’re committed to working closely with Bolt to ensure responsible data handling as the program evolves.
Best regards,

Tested initial protocol on following use case

* “IoT devkit“ MCU sends vehicle state (speed, soc, time, turn) every 100ms on channel 1 to display
* “IoT devkit“ MCU sends images continuously on channel 10, if BOOT button is not pressed, to display
* Display MCU renders MVP html with provided vehicle state
* Display MCU renders and scrolls image

SPI is set to HD, 40 MHz, 1-bit

SPI data fragmentation is set to 1024 bytes

Display command TX jitter is ~10 ms with no image upload, ~10 ms while images were sent

Display command RX jitter is related to FPS, which was 1/0.120 Hz with no image upload, 1/0.220 Hz while images were sent

Images are 7kb PNGs, which take ~3 ms to receive

According to this test it takes 90% CPU to handle 35 Mbit/s SPI

Data overflow occurs on channel 10 most of the time
